title: Pommes boulangère
subtitle: Thinly sliced potatoes baked in stock with onions
excerpt: Sliced potatoes and onions layered and baked slowly in meat or vegetable stock until tender and golden on top. A leaner alternative to gratin dauphinois, traditionally baked in the residual heat of a baker's oven.
sourceNotes: Pommes boulangère is a traditional French dish whose name refers to the practice of taking it to the local baker's oven (boulangerie) to cook in the residual heat after bread had been baked. It appears in Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire (1903) and in Larousse Gastronomique (1938). Both are in the public domain or widely available as historical reference works.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be assembled the evening before, covered, and refrigerated. Add an extra 10 minutes to the cooking time if baking from cold.

content.text: Pommes boulangère is what you cook when you want the comfort of a potato gratin without the cream. The potatoes soak up the stock as they cook, becoming silky and flavourful. The top layer browns and crisps in the oven heat. It is good alongside a leg of lamb or a roast chicken, and needs nothing else on the plate.

items.prepNote: waxy variety, peeled and very thinly sliced (2 to 3 mm)
hot; vegetable stock works equally well
for the dish and the top layer

content.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (fan 160°C). Butter a large, shallow baking dish or roasting tin generously.

Arrange a layer of potato slices in the base, overlapping them slightly like roof tiles. Season with salt and pepper, scatter over some onion slices and a little thyme. Continue layering until all the potato and onion are used, seasoning each layer. Finish with a neat top layer of potato.
Pour the hot stock over the layers; it should come just below the top layer of potato. Dot the surface with the remaining butter.

Bake for 1 hour to 1 hour 20 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender when pierced with a knife and the top is golden brown. If the top browns too quickly, lay a sheet of foil loosely over the dish.
Leave to rest for 10 minutes before serving. The stock will have been almost entirely absorbed.

items.cause: Slices were too thick, or the dish was crowded
items.fix: Slice to 2 to 3 mm maximum. A mandoline helps. Continue baking, covered with foil, until tender.

items.symptom: Stock absorbed before potatoes are cooked
items.cause: Not enough stock, or the dish is too large and stock spread too thin
items.fix: Add more hot stock, 100 ml at a time, until the potatoes finish cooking.

items.cause: Oven temperature too low, or dish placed too low in the oven
items.fix: Move to the top third of the oven for the last 15 minutes. A few minutes under the grill finishes it well.

content.text: Pommes boulangère is the French provincial alternative to the richer gratin dauphinois. It is classically paired with lamb, particularly gigot d'agneau, where the meat and potatoes often cook together in the same pan, the lamb juices dripping down into the potato layers. It is dairy-free, which makes it a useful thing to know when cooking for guests who do not eat cream.
